Sparse attention fixes memory bandwidth, not memory capacity.

“The whole idea of HiCache is trying to offload KV cache from the HBM to a lower tier, higher capacity but lower bandwidth memory, and only load the most relevant set of tokens during computation.”

“Sparse attention doesn’t mitigate the memory capacity bottleneck. It’s a technique that helps a lot with memory bandwidth.”

“During the sparse attention computation, you still need to select the tokens. So you still have to keep all the tokens in context, and you cannot discard them. At some point, it still has to be loaded into HBM.”

“That’s where HiSparse becomes useful, because it can apply the typical caching rules so that you could load the most relevant parts into HBM.”

A couple of decades ago, the chances of surviving more than ten years with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were slim. Today, thanks to antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV/AIDS can expect to live long lives. ART is a mixture of antiviral drugs that are used to treat people infected with HIV. It is an essential player in making progress against HIV/AIDS because it saves lives, allows patients to live longer, and prevents new infections.

Since the first version of ART was introduced in the late 1980s, the treatment has saved millions of lives. The chart shows the annual number of deaths from HIV/AIDS and the number of deaths averted as a result of ART. Today, a person living in a high-income country who started ART in their twenties can expect to live for another 46 years — that is, well into their 60s.

There is considerable evidence to show that people who use ART are less likely to transmit HIV to another person. ART reduces the number of viral particles present in an HIV-positive individual, and therefore, the likelihood of passing the virus to another person decreases. In 2011, the journal Science named as its “Breakthrough of the Year” a study that found that ART reduced the risk of HIV transmission between couples by 96%.

The number of people who receive ART has increased significantly in recent years. But to make progress against HIV/AIDS and fully benefit from the potential of ART treatment, we need to increase HIV/AIDS awareness and improve access to ART.

What if robots could learn from millions of videos instead of relying on more limited teleoperation data?

Today, much of robot learning still depends on humans remotely controlling robots to collect training data. It’s expensive, time-consuming, and the resulting policies often struggle when robots encounter unfamiliar environments.

@RhodaAI is working on a different approach.

The team is training robot foundation models on internet-scale video, using footage of the physical world to help robots learn how objects move and interact.

But processing that much video comes with a serious infrastructure challenge.

@nebiusai is a cloud platform designed for exactly these kinds of physical AI workloads. Rhoda recently shared how working with Nebius helped them double their compute capacity at a critical stage of development.

What I found particularly interesting was how much emphasis the team placed on reliability.

Beyond GPU capacity, Rhoda needed a cluster that could reliably train large models, managed Kubernetes and Slurm to orchestrate workloads, and petabyte-scale storage located close to its compute resources.

Nebius worked with the team to put that infrastructure in place.

This allowed Rhoda to train on video and teleoperation data much more efficiently, significantly reducing downtime for both infrastructure and researchers.

It’s an interesting look at what it takes to train robots at this scale, and why the infrastructure behind physical AI deserves more attention.

I’ll be joining the @nebiusai team at NVIDIA GTC Berlin next week. Looking forward to seeing what they’re building for physical AI, and thanks to @nvidia for the invitation!

瑞银：现在是买入A股的好时机吗？

瑞银在10月14日发布《中国股票策略：现在是买入A股的好时机吗？》。报告指出，近期A股回调主要因科技板块拥挤仓位平仓，但下行风险有限，盈利仍在上行周期。以下内容整理自该报告。

1、近期回调与7月不同

9月底以来，A股尤其是科技板块快速回调。融资余额收缩、成交低迷，显示投资者情绪疲弱。瑞银认为，本轮走弱与7月不同。

7月回调由全球科技叙事降温和快速去杠杆触发，而近期回调更多是科技板块拥挤仓位集中平仓所致，同时公募基金面临回本赎回压力。

地缘政治、美债收益率和油价波动也通过通胀预期收紧美元流动性，压制风险偏好。

2、ETF在关键点位持续流入

瑞银指出，主要宽基ETF自上周五以来成交额快速放大。自2024年以来，每当上证综指快速跌破关键点位，2024年3000点、2025年3200点、2026年3800点，ETF都录得流入。

与2024至25年ETF流入主要集中在沪深300不同，近期流入更广泛分布在沪深300、中证500、中证1000、创业板和科创50 ETF。因此瑞银认为A股下行风险有限。

事实上，A股盈利仍处在上行周期，二季度全A盈利增速加速至29.4%，一季度为9.3%，上半年盈利增长19.5%。瑞银预计2026年全年全A盈利增长15%。尽管近期回调，市场一致盈利预测仍维持高位。

3、科技拥挤度已大幅缓解

从交易数据看，广义科技板块周成交额占全A比重已回落至今年4月初水平，当前37.2%，远低于7月初的历史峰值49.7%。换手率最高的前1%、前5%和前10%股票成交占比也降至4月初水平。

这表明尾部风险和仓位拥挤已基本释放。不过，场外资金快速回流近期不太可能，因投资者风险偏好恢复需要时间。

公募基金二季报显示，广义科技板块超配比例升至18.5%的历史新高，超过2015年四季度16.2%的前高。

但随着监管对“广义基金集中行业暴露”的控制，公募基金可能已在三季度调仓。

4、投资建议

大家以為台積電的封裝還缺到卡住客戶，其實這次法說，魏哲家的口氣放軟了。

7 月法說，他說封裝產能不足，「已成為支援客戶的瓶頸」，還歡迎其他家的方案來分擔。這次被問到，他的說法是後段「確實有一點短缺」。

從「瓶頸」變成「有一點」，CoWoS 產能數字一樣沒給。

被問到英特爾 EMIB，如果對手交不出貨，台積電要不要接？他沒正面回答，只說「讓客戶產品順利上市是第一優先」，還補一句：這樣暗示夠了。

缺口沒消失，是有人幫忙補。我昨天寫格芯馬爾他，講的是日本出錢的那兩座廠。同一個馬爾他還有另一張單：格芯 10/8 公告，跟台積電簽 20 億美元、5 年的矽中介層合約，2028 年上半年開始放量。

中介層就是 CoWoS 底下那塊矽板，GPU 和 HBM 都坐在上面。台積電把它外包一部分到紐約，等於把最緊的那一段，交給別人一起做。

板子還會越來越大。現在量產的是 5 倍光罩尺寸，9 倍、14 倍在開發，另外推 CoPoS 想把成本壓下來。但他說，現在客戶的首選還是 CoWoS。

📰 $INFQ / $QNT | Morgan Stanley's Quantum Valuations: I'm Not Buying It. Neither Should You, In My Opinion.

@MorganStanley @MgnStnlyIdeas

Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore initiated coverage of $INFQ on October 15 with an Equal-Weight rating and a $12 price target, while upgrading $QNT to Overweight with a $62 target.

And here's something investors should know.

Morgan Stanley served as a joint lead underwriter of QNT's $1.68 BILLION IPO in June 2026. Four months later, the firm identifies QNT as its preferred quantum investment, arguing that it trades at the lowest multiple of projected 2030 revenue among its peers.

That relationship doesn't automatically invalidate the research. But I believe it deserves scrutiny.

I'm not buying it. Here's why.

1. THE VALUATION DISCONNECT

Several months ago, I published a comparative financial analysis of seven publicly traded quantum companies.

My historical figures showed:

📊 Market Cap / TTM Revenue

$INFQ: 109.1× 
$IONQ: 130.3× 
$QNT: 920.6×

💰 Estimated TTM Operating Cash Burn

INFQ: $47.5M 
QNT: $190.4M

📊 Q1 Revenue / Operating Cash Burn

INFQ: 0.49× 
IONQ: 0.43× 
QNT: 0.08×

At the time, QNT traded at approximately 8.4× INFQ's trailing revenue multiple, while consuming roughly four times as much operating cash.

Morgan Stanley is using projected 2030 revenue rather than historical financials. I understand the distinction. 

But what assumptions justify reversing such a substantial historical valuation disparity?

What revenue growth, commercialization timelines, capital requirements, and dilution assumptions support that conclusion?

2. "BUT QNT IS SO FAR AHEAD!"
I can already hear this argument.

And I'll acknowledge something upfront.

QNT has demonstrated leadership in several important areas of quantum computing, particularly fault-tolerance demonstrations, logical-qubit performance, and aspects of its technical roadmap.

I recognize that.

But technical leadership isn't a single measurement, and it certainly isn't the same thing as financial valuation.

INFQ has its own technological strengths involving neutral-atom architecture, connectivity, logical-qubit demonstrations, software, and chip-scale hardware development.

Its recent 30-logical-qubit demonstration deserves serious consideration, including an honest examination of its error-detection and post-selection limitations.

And its software and hardware development programs could become important competitive differentiators.

So here's my question: How much is QNT's technical advantage actually worth in 2030 revenue?

Morgan Stanley reportedly projects:

QNT 2028 Revenue: ~$270 MILLION

QNT 2030 Revenue: ~$2 BILLION

That's approximately 7.4× revenue growth in just two years.

An extraordinary forecast.

What assumptions support that trajectory?

How much depends on commercially viable fault-tolerant computing?

What probability is assigned to achieving those milestones?

What are the expected margins, capital requirements, and dilution?

And perhaps most importantly:

What are the equivalent 2030 revenue projections for INFQ?

Because if you're going to project extraordinary commercialization success several years into the future, you need to explain how those technical advantages translate into customers, contracts, revenue, and ultimately shareholder value.

You can't simply say QNT is ahead and treat the valuation question as settled.

3. QUANTUM SENSING: MY BIGGEST CONCERN

INFQ IS NOT JUST A QUANTUM COMPUTING COMPANY.

And this is where I seriously question whether Morgan Stanley's valuation captures the full opportunity.

Boston Consulting Group has projected a $3–$5 BILLION quantum sensing market by 2030.

Bank of America has separately discussed a quantum sensing market potentially reaching approximately $6 BILLION by 2035.

Now, Joseph Moore, you're willing to project quantum computing revenues all the way out to 2030.

Fine.

Then why shouldn't we apply that same forward-looking framework to quantum sensing?

Even if we take the lower end of BCG's $3 billion estimate and cut it by 75%, we're still looking at a potential $750 MILLION market.

And INFQ is already an established participant in this field.

Its portfolio includes:

• Quantum inertial navigation 
• GPS-independent navigation technologies 
• Quantum RF sensing 
• Precision timing and atomic clocks 
• Quantum gravity sensing 
• Defense and aerospace applications

These technologies have commercialization pathways that differ from fault-tolerant quantum computing. Some already have commercial products, government customers, and established development programs.

So where is quantum sensing in your 2030 revenue model?

What market share are you assigning INFQ?

What adoption rates are you assuming?

How are you accounting for its existing products, government relationships, and commercial development programs?

I'm not claiming Morgan Stanley excluded quantum sensing. I haven't reviewed the complete underlying model. But if your $12 valuation meaningfully incorporates this opportunity, I'd like to see the assumptions.

And yes, TAM is not company revenue. Market share, margins, execution, and dilution matter. That's precisely why the underlying numbers are so important.

4. WHAT ABOUT INFQ'S QUANTUM COMPUTING R&D?

Infleqtion's neutral-atom architecture, logical-qubit demonstrations, error-correction research, and commercial partnerships deserve serious technical consideration.

QNT has demonstrated substantial progress in fault tolerance. I recognize that.

But INFQ's neutral-atom approach offers a different set of potential advantages in scalability, connectivity, and architecture.

Its research also extends into software and hardware miniaturization, areas that could become increasingly important as quantum systems move toward commercial deployment.

Has Morgan Stanley adequately assessed INFQ's technical roadmap and long-term commercialization potential?

Or is its valuation disproportionately rewarding QNT's current technical leadership while discounting the potential of competing architectures?

And how are those technological differences being translated into actual financial forecasts?

That's what I want to understand.

5. THE TIMING. YOU REALLY CAN'T MAKE THIS UP.

I've been calling for Morgan Stanley to initiate coverage of INFQ for months.

MONTHS.

And when do they finally show up?

After macroeconomic selling has already inflicted substantial damage on INFQ's share price.

They initiate coverage at $12.

Meanwhile, QNT gets upgraded to Overweight and named their preferred quantum investment.

The same QNT Morgan Stanley helped take public just four months ago.

You really can't make this stuff up.

I've been waiting for Morgan Stanley to take a serious look at INFQ's underlying technology, particularly its quantum sensing portfolio and neutral-atom computing research.

Instead, the timing raises more questions for me than it answers.

I'm not alleging the report was deliberately timed or that the underwriting relationship influenced the analyst's conclusions. I have no evidence establishing either.

But investors are entitled to question the timing, the methodology, and potential conflicts of interest.

You initiate coverage after macro conditions have beaten down INFQ, assign one of the lowest targets on the Street, and simultaneously upgrade a company your firm helped bring public?

Then tell us that company is the most attractively valued quantum investment based on projected 2030 revenue?

Sorry, Morgan Stanley. Still not buying it.

6. MY INFQ THESIS REMAINS INTACT

My investment thesis has never rested exclusively on quantum computing.

It rests on Infleqtion's broader portfolio of quantum computing, sensing, navigation, precision timing, and national security technologies.

I recognize that all these businesses carry commercialization and execution risks.

But I also believe their potential deserves serious consideration in any long-term valuation.

If Morgan Stanley has thoroughly modeled INFQ's sensing portfolio and neutral-atom computing research and still arrives at $12, I'd genuinely like to understand the assumptions.

Because right now, I have more questions than answers.

Morgan Stanley helped underwrite QNT's IPO.

Four months later, it upgrades QNT while initiating INFQ at $12, following substantial macro-driven selling pressure.

Meanwhile, INFQ participates in a potentially multibillion-dollar quantum sensing market that deserves explicit consideration in any serious 2030 valuation model.

The underwriting relationship is documented.

The timing is observable.

The quantum sensing market opportunity is supported by independent research.

And the valuation methodology deserves examination.

Until then, I'll continue following the technology, financials, and commercial developments rather than relying solely on institutional price targets.

Still not buying it.

My opinion. My research. Not financial advice.

CFR asked members of the Society for Historians of American Foreign Relations what they considered to be the best and worst foreign policy decisions in U.S. history.

A U.S. Air Force surveillance flight over Cuba in October 1962 turned up evidence of what U.S. officials had feared: the Soviet Union was installing nuclear-armed missiles on the island. The discovery triggered a 13-day crisis, beginning on October 16, that brought the world to the brink of nuclear war.
